job.text: soft-skinned--of that peculiar shade of grey which I have seen only in Cornwall. And, being rather a connoisseur in cows, I have often amused myself to notice how the kine of each country have their own predominant colour, which seems to harmonise with its special landscape. The curious yellow tint of Highland cattle, the red, white, or brown of those of the midland counties, and the delicate grey of Cornish cows, alike suit the scene around them, and belong to it as completely as the dainty little Swiss herds do to their Alpine pastures, or the large, mild, cream- oxen to the Campagna at Rome. But we had to tear ourselves away from this Arcadia, for in the midst of the farm-yard appeared the carriage and Charles. So we jolted back--it seemed as if Cornish carriages and horses could go anywhere and over everything--to the Old Inn and Mary Mundy. She _had_ come home, and everything was right. As we soon found, everything and everybody was accustomed to be put to rights by Miss Mary Mundy. She stood at the door to greet us--a bright, brown-faced little woman with the reddest of cheeks and the blackest of eyes
